output.query: migrainous infarction criteria and antiplatelet secondary prevention after minor ischaemic stroke

results.finding: Migrainous infarction (1.4.3): one or more aura symptoms associated with an ischaemic brain lesion in the appropriate territory demonstrated by neuroimaging, in a patient with migraine with aura, during an attack typical of previous attacks except that aura symptoms persist for more than 60 minutes, and not better accounted for by another diagnosis. Persistent aura without infarction is 1.4.2.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

results.finding: After minor non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke, dual antiplatelet therapy started within 24 hours and continued for 21-90 days reduces early recurrence; thereafter a single antiplatelet agent is recommended for long-term prevention.
results.source: Kleindorfer DO, Towfighi A, Chaturvedi S, et al. 2021 Guideline for the prevention of stroke in patients with stroke and transient ischemic attack. Stroke 2021;52:e364-e467

output.summary: Migrainous infarction requires an infarct in the aura territory during an otherwise typical attack with aura over 60 minutes; after a minor stroke, short-term early dual antiplatelet therapy is followed by single-agent prevention.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ten-year typical visual aura history; index attack typical except the left-field aura persisted about 5 h; no neck pain, thunderclap onset or palpitations; sumatriptan taken since; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and SNNOOP10 red-flag review, applying ICHD-3 1.2 and 1.4.3
action_criteria.rationale: Migrainous infarction is defined clinically before it is confirmed by imaging: the index attack must be typical of her previous attacks except that the aura persists beyond 60 minutes (ICHD-3 1.4.3). The history also screens for other stroke mechanisms (dissection, RCVS, cardiac) and records the drugs that need review.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: 4 mm subacute cortical infarct in the right occipital cortex at the site of the outside DWI lesion; no other lesion
action_criteria.label: Repeat brain MRI to confirm the infarct and its location against the aura
action_criteria.rationale: ICHD-3 1.4.3 criterion C requires an ischaemic infarct in the area relevant to the aura (right occipital cortex for a left-field aura); the outside report is not available, so the study is repeated and compared.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal intracranial and cervical arteries: no PCA or vertebral stenosis, dissection or segmental narrowing
action_criteria.label: MR angiography of the head and neck to exclude dissection, stenosis and vasculopathy
action_criteria.rationale: Migrainous infarction is a diagnosis of exclusion (criterion D): vertebral artery dissection, posterior circulation stenosis and RCVS cause occipital infarcts in young adults and must be excluded with vessel imaging.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lupus anticoagulant negative, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I below 20 U; ESR and CRP normal; HbA1c and lipids normal
action_criteria.label: Antiphospholipid antibodies, inflammatory markers and vascular risk bloods in a young woman with stroke
action_criteria.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome is a treatable cause of arterial stroke in young women that would change secondary prevention; recommended rather than required because she has no history of thrombosis or pregnancy loss.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No AF or flutter over 30 days; sinus rhythm during symptomatic events
action_criteria.label: 30-day ambulatory ECG monitoring for paroxysmal AF
action_criteria.rationale: Paroxysmal AF is a cardioembolic mechanism that must be excluded before an infarct is attributed to migraine; prolonged monitoring detects more AF than 24-48 h recordings.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cardiac structure and function; no thrombus; no right-to-left shunt at rest or with Valsalva
action_criteria.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram with agitated saline (bubble study)
action_criteria.rationale: A cryptogenic-appearing stroke under 60 needs a structural cardiac source and a PFO excluded; a PFO with a high-risk anatomy would change management, unlike PFO screening in migraine alone.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Triptans contraindicated after stroke; NSAID with antiplatelets adds bleeding risk; POP after stroke UKMEC 3, copper IUD UKMEC 1
action_criteria.label: Check sumatriptan, the dual antiplatelet therapy and her progestogen-only pill after the stroke
action_criteria.rationale: Required: she is still taking sumatriptan after an ischaemic stroke, is on dual antiplatelet therapy and takes a progestogen-only pill whose category changes after stroke; each changes management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on ICHD-3 1.4.3 and antiplatelet duration after minor stroke
action_criteria.label: Literature on migrainous infarction criteria and secondary prevention
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or restart triptans or ergot derivatives after migrainous infarction.
Do not continue dual antiplatelet therapy long term.
Do not start anticoagulation: there is no AF, cardiac thrombus or antiphospholipid syndrome.
Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): it is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura and after stroke; offer a copper IUD or an LNG-IUS.
required_recommendations: Explain the diagnosis: migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3), an attack typical of her aura except that it persisted about 5 hours, with a small right occipital cortical infarct in the corresponding area and no other mechanism on MRA, 30-day monitoring, bubble echo and antiphospholipid testing.

Stop sumatriptan permanently (triptans are contraindicated after stroke); treat attacks at headache onset with naproxen 500 mg and an antiemetic, with a proton pump inhibitor if NSAIDs are used often on antiplatelet therapy.

Stop dual antiplatelet therapy and continue a single antiplatelet agent long term (clopidogrel 75 mg or aspirin 75 mg): DAPT benefit after minor stroke applies when started within 24 hours and limited to 21-90 days (AHA/ASA 2021).

Start migraine prevention (2-4 attacks a month after a migrainous infarction): candesartan (fetotoxic: only with reliable contraception), propranolol or amitriptyline; if topiramate is chosen, start it only with highly effective contraception (copper or hormonal IUD, or implant) under the topiramate pregnancy prevention programme; it reduces the efficacy of oral and progestogen-only pills.
Review contraception: after stroke, continuing the progestogen-only pill is UKMEC category 3; offer a copper IUD (UKMEC 1) or an LNG-IUS (UKMEC 2).

Driving (DVLA group 1): she must not drive for 1 month after the stroke and may resume if recovery is complete with no visual field defect; she need not notify the DVLA unless a deficit persists after 1 month.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

accepted: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3) — small right occipital cortical infarct during established visual aura; all secondary causes excluded; DAPT not indicated long-term

differential.key_features: No neck pain or trauma; normal intracranial and cervical MRA.
No thunderclap headache; the attack matched her usual migraine; no segmental narrowing on MRA.
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I negative; no history of thrombosis or pregnancy loss.
Excluded by definition: imaging shows an infarct in the aura territory, and the aura resolved within hours, not over a week.

key_clinical_evidence: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3) requires an attack typical of previous auras except that an aura symptom lasts over 60 minutes, an infarct in the corresponding area, and no better explanation; a 20-minute aura with an infarct does not qualify.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion: vessel imaging, prolonged cardiac monitoring, bubble echo and antiphospholipid testing must be negative.
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated permanently after the infarct.
DAPT after minor stroke applies when started within 24 hours and for 21-90 days; long-term prevention is a single antiplatelet agent.
After stroke, combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 and continuing a progestogen-only pill UKMEC 3; a copper IUD is UKMEC 1.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: DAPT was started about 3 days after the event, outside the 24-hour window in which AHA/ASA 2021 recommends DAPT after minor stroke, and is now 4 weeks in; a single antiplatelet agent is the long-term regimen.
red_herrings.data_point: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) started by the local team
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be taken as an ongoing indication to continue both agents

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An infarct in the aura territory during a prolonged but otherwise typical aura is migrainous infarction only after other mechanisms are excluded; the work-up finds no cardioembolic, arterial or prothrombotic cause, so anticoagulation is not indicated.
red_herrings.data_point: Outside MRI reported as a small stroke
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead to labelling the event as an ordinary ischaemic stroke and stopping the work-up at the infarct, or to anticoagulation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The POP is UKMEC 2 in migraine with aura alone, but after stroke continuing it is UKMEC 3; a copper IUD or LNG-IUS is preferred.
red_herrings.data_point: On a progestogen-only pill (Cerazette), switched from the combined pill because of migraine with aura
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead to continuing desogestrel without review after the stroke

The infarct location defines the arterial territory the vessel study must examine.
Cardiac monitoring is the stroke-mechanism work-up of an infarct confirmed on MRI.
The bubble echo is the stroke-mechanism work-up of an infarct confirmed on MRI.

findings.result: Migraine with visual aura for 10 years, 2-4 attacks a month; usual aura a left-field shimmering zigzag spreading over 15-25 min and clearing within 30 min, followed by right-sided headache. Two typical attacks since the index attack.

Began as her usual aura, spreading over 20 min, with a 12 h right-sided headache; a blurred flickering patch in the left visual field then persisted for about 5 h before resolving fully. No weakness, numbness, speech or brainstem symptoms.
Visual only; positive; unilateral (left field); gradual spread; 15-25 min; headache within 60 min. No succession of other modalities.
No neck pain or trauma, no thunderclap onset, no palpitations, no previous thrombosis or pregnancy loss, no systemic symptoms. Non-smoker. Combined pill stopped 10 years ago; on desogestrel.
Clopidogrel 75 mg and aspirin 75 mg started by the local team after the outside MRI (about day 3); sumatriptan 100 mg taken for the two attacks since; desogestrel 75 micrograms daily.
Normal neurological examination: visual acuity 6/6, full visual fields to confrontation, no focal deficit; BP 118/74 mmHg, regular pulse 70, no murmur or carotid bruit.

Aura lasting over 60 min: present (index attack). Reported infarct on outside imaging: present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, persisting deficit, thunderclap onset, onset over 50, positional features, papilloedema, painful eye, trauma and medication overuse: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. Usual attacks meet ICHD-3 1.2.1 migraine with typical aura (5 of 6 C characteristics). 2. The index attack was typical of her previous attacks except that the visual aura persisted for about 5 hours, fulfilling the clinical part of migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3); an infarct in the corresponding area must be shown on imaging and other stroke mechanisms excluded. A 5-hour aura is too short for persistent aura without infarction (1.4.2, one week or more). 3. Normal examination today.

alternatives: Acute: naproxen 500 mg with an antiemetic (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine) at headache onset; a gepant (for example rimegepant) has no vasoconstrictor activity and can be used where triptans are contraindicated, with limited data after stroke.
Preventive: candesartan, propranolol or amitriptyline; topiramate only under the pregnancy prevention programme.
contraindications: Triptans (all 5-HT1B/1D agonists) are contraindicated after stroke or TIA, including migrainous infarction (SmPC), because of their vasoconstrictor action.
Ergotamine and other ergot derivatives: contraindicated for the same reason.
interactions: Sumatriptan with clopidogrel or aspirin: no pharmacokinetic interaction.
Sumatriptan with desogestrel: no clinically significant interaction.
Clopidogrel with aspirin: additive bleeding risk; dual therapy beyond the early weeks after a minor stroke increases bleeding without further reduction in recurrence.

NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen) with clopidogrel or aspirin: additive gastrointestinal bleeding risk; consider a proton pump inhibitor if used often (lansoprazole or pantoprazole rather than omeprazole or esomeprazole with clopidogrel).
Topiramate with desogestrel: enzyme induction at doses of 200 mg/day or more can reduce the contraceptive effect of progestogen-only pills.
sumatriptan.proposed: sumatriptan 100 mg as needed, with clopidogrel 75 mg, aspirin 75 mg and desogestrel 75 micrograms
sumatriptan.summary: Sumatriptan is contraindicated after an ischaemic stroke; NSAIDs with antiplatelet therapy add bleeding risk. Sources: sumatriptan, clopidogrel and desogestrel SmPC; BNF; UKMEC 2025.
warnings: Combined oestrogen-containing contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura and after stroke.
Progestogen-only pill after stroke: UKMEC category 3 to continue; copper IUD category 1, LNG-IUS category 2.
Topiramate is subject to a pregnancy prevention programme: highly effective contraception (IUD or implant) is required.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 38-year-old Indian-British woman attends the neurology outpatient clinic for a second opinion 4 weeks after an unusual migraine attack. The attack began like her usual ones: a shimmering zigzag arc in her left peripheral field that expanded over about 20 minutes, followed by a severe right-sided headache lasting 12 hours. Unlike her usual auras, the visual disturbance did not clear: a blurred, flickering patch in the left field persisted for about 5 hours before resolving completely that evening. Worried by this, she attended a walk-in centre the next day, and an MRI was performed at an outside hospital 3 days after the attack. She was told it showed a small stroke, and the local team started clopidogrel 75 mg and aspirin 75 mg daily. The outside report is not with her today.

She has a 10-year history of migraine with visual aura, with 2-4 attacks a month, all with a typical expanding visual aura lasting 15-25 minutes followed by right-sided headache; before this attack her aura had always cleared within half an hour. She has had two typical attacks since, each with a 20-minute aura that cleared fully, and treated the headaches with sumatriptan 100 mg. She had a combined OCP stopped 10 years ago when her migraines were first diagnosed and is now on a progestogen-only pill (Cerazette). She has no neck pain or trauma and no palpitations. She is very concerned about the diagnosis and is currently not driving (advised by the previous team).
